name: Copy edit with a change list
summary: Hand over a page, an email or a brochure and get it back plainer and tighter, with no claim stronger than the statements you can support and a change list that shows every edit, its reason and any meaning it moved. You approve each change before the copy is used.

sources.title: Fully Powered AI's own copy-editing guide and its rules for claims: every claim held to what the company can support before any polish, never strengthened, and every change recorded for a person to approve.

sources.contribution: The method the guide rewrites: editing in separate passes, each on one quality, with earlier passes rechecked after every one; the passes for clarity, one consistent voice, what each line means for the reader, and specific facts in place of vague words, including dropping a sentence that cannot be made specific; the list of habits that make copy read as machine-written (the turn-around contrast, the run of absences, the self-answered question and staged reveal, stock openers, the restating tail clause, praise words standing in for facts, dashes in headings and other short lines); fixing such a habit from the fact rather than a synonym; finding each claim in the copy and flagging the ones without support; marking a missing fact for someone to supply rather than making it up; a reason for every edit; and keeping the author's message, with the author deciding.

Asking, before editing, where the copy will appear and who reads it; house-style switches that turn a habit off when the brand uses it on purpose; four further habits to fix (a verbless phrase standing in for a full sentence, a sentence that hinges on "so", a sentence that opens with a label before making its point, a blanket closing line beginning "none of that"); a report listing each edit that altered what the copy says, however small; re-reading after the fixes so that one repair is not repeated until it becomes a habit of its own; and leaving headlines and lines the owner has signed off exactly as they are.
A verdict at the top on one of three levels (ready as it stands; nearly there, with named items to fix; not ready until a basic problem is settled), and the rule that the verdict is never softened.
